entities.name: Chlothar II
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Chlothar II (584–629 CE), often referred to as 'the Young,' was a pivotal Merovingian monarch whose reign marked the temporary reunification of the Frankish kingdoms after decades of brutal internecine warfare. Born into the Neustrian royal line, he ascended to the throne of Neustria as an infant following the assassination of his father, Chilperic I, in 584 CE. His early years were dominated by the regency of his mother, Fredegund, and the continuing, bloody feuds with his aunt Brunhild, the formidable queen dowager of Austrasia and later Burgundy. Chlothar’s ultimate triumph over Brunhild in 613 CE allowed him to consolidate power across Neustria, Austrasia, and Burgundy, effectively reuniting Francia under a single ruler for the first time since the reign of his grandfather, Chlothar I.

His reign was characterized by a complex interplay between royal authority and the rising power of the Frankish aristocracy. After his decisive victory over Brunhild, Chlothar II issued the Edict of Paris in 614 CE, a landmark legal document that granted significant privileges and autonomy to the nobility, particularly in Austrasia and Burgundy. This edict, often interpreted as a concession to those who aided his victory, allowed local magnates to consolidate their power and influence, laying the groundwork for the later ascendancy of the Mayors of the Palace. He also engaged in military campaigns against the Saxons, securing the eastern frontiers, and maintained a degree of peace within his vast realm, albeit through a decentralized administrative structure that empowered regional lords.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Chlothar II's reign temporarily reunited the fragmented Frankish kingdoms, ending decades of civil war, and his Edict of Paris fundamentally reshaped the balance of power by significantly empowering the Frankish aristocracy, laying the groundwork for the Carolingian ascendancy.
